claim: Open Science Collaboration (2015) replicated 100 studies from three psychology journals.
value: 97% of originals significant vs 36% of replications; 'Replication effects were half the magnitude of original effects'; 47% of original effect sizes inside replication 95% CI; 39% subjectively rated as replicated
source: Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science, 349(6251), aac4716.
caveat: 2026-11-14 re-check: 97%/36% confirmed by BPS Research Digest and PsyPost summaries. Some summaries say 35/100 significant after exclusions. 'Replicated' depends on the criterion used.

claim: Hagger et al. (2016) 23-lab preregistered replication of the sequential-task ego-depletion effect.
value: 23 labs; N = 2,141; d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15] (earlier meta-analytic estimate d = 0.62)
source: Hagger, M. S., Chatzisarantis, N. L. D., et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546-573.
caveat: 2026-11-14 re-check confirmed 23 labs, N = 2,141, d = 0.04 [-0.07, 0.15] (Discover; Massey/Tilburg repositories). Baumeister & Vohs disputed the task choice; the RRR tests one paradigm, not every form of self-control fatigue.

claim: Le Texier (2019) re-examined the Stanford Prison Experiment using archives and interviews.
value: Archive study + interviews with 15 participants; guards received instructions; demand characteristics; biased/incomplete data collection
source: Le Texier, T. (2019). Debunking the Stanford Prison Experiment. American Psychologist, 74(7), 823-839. PMID 31380664.
caveat: 2026-11-14 re-check confirmed citation, DOI and 15 interviews (CAS catalogue; Gwern-hosted PDF). A reply appeared in Am Psychol 2020, 75(3), 400-402 (Zimbardo & Haney per seed research; authorship not re-confirmed this pass).

claim: Milgram (1963) baseline obedience study at Yale.
value: 26 of 40 men (65%) continued to 450 V; none stopped before 300 V; one condition only
source: Milgram, S. (1963). Behavioral study of obedience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(4), 371-378.
caveat: Seed row verified by orchestrator research (PubMed/primary); a single condition with a male US sample; never present 65% as a universal obedience rate. Archival work (Perry; Haslam et al.) documents protocol deviations.

claim: Haslam, Loughnan & Perry (2014) synthesised Milgram's obedience conditions.
value: 21 conditions in which obedience = progression to maximum voltage; N = 740; overall obedience 43.6% (range across conditions 0-92.5%)
source: Haslam, N., Loughnan, S., & Perry, G. (2014). Meta-Milgram: An empirical synthesis of the obedience experiments. PLOS ONE, 9(4), e93927.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (PLOS ONE record + Univ. Melbourne repository + Social Science Space). Milgram ran 23 small-sample conditions in total; other pooled figures (37.5%, ~43%) depend on which conditions are included.

claim: Miller's (2009) commentary on Burger's replication.
value: Burger reported 'a high base rate of obedience, comparable to that observed by Stanley Milgram'
source: Miller, A. G. (2009). Reflections on 'Replicating Milgram' (Burger, 2009). American Psychologist, 64(1), 20-27.
caveat: Seed row verified by orchestrator research (PubMed/primary); quote taken from the PubMed abstract during seed research; not re-fetched 2026-11-14.

claim: Burger (2009) partial replication of Milgram using a '150-volt solution' (session stopped at the first verbal protest).
value: N = 70 adults (29 men, 41 women); 70% of base-condition participants continued past 150 V vs 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition (difference not significant); 63% continued in a modelled-refusal condition
source: Burger, J. M. (2009). Replicating Milgram: Would people still obey today? American Psychologist, 64(1), 1-11.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 via APA press release, ScienceDaily and Time (3 independent reports of Burger's own figures). Per-condition n (base vs modelled refusal) not confirmed. Commentaries in the same issue (e.g., Elms, 'Obedience lite') question comparability with Milgram.

claim: Baumrind (1964) published an early ethics critique of Milgram (1963).
value: Critique of deception, distress and inadequate protection of participants
source: Baumrind, D. (1964). Some thoughts on ethics of research: After reading Milgram's 'Behavioral Study of Obedience'. American Psychologist, 19(6), 421-423.
caveat: Not searched online this pass; citation from bibliographic knowledge. Verify volume/pages/DOI before UI use.

claim: Asch line-judgement conformity studies (1951/1955/1956).
value: 123 male students in the 1956 monograph; 12 critical trials; ~36.8% of critical-trial responses conformed (mean ~4.4/12); ~75% conformed at least once; ~24-25% never conformed
source: Asch, S. E. (1956). Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority. Psychological Monographs, 70(9), 1-70.
caveat: 2026-11-14: several secondary summaries agree on ~37% / ~75% / ~25% but the primary monograph was not reachable; the 1955 and 1956 samples may overlap; '74%' also appears. Show only with 'figure under verification' badge.

claim: Bond & Smith (1996) meta-analysis of Asch-type line-judgement studies.
value: 133 studies from 17 countries; conformity higher in collectivist cultures; declined in US studies since the 1950s
source: Bond, R., & Smith, P. B. (1996). Culture and conformity: A meta-analysis of studies using Asch's (1952b, 1956) line judgment task. Psychological Bulletin, 119(1), 111-137.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (ProQuest record + FORRT open textbook chapter). Pooled N reported by blogs (24,617) not confirmed.

claim: Simons & Chabris (1999) sustained inattentional blindness ('gorilla') study.
value: N = 192 analysed; 46% failed to notice the unexpected event; gorilla noticed 44% vs umbrella woman 65%; easy task 64% vs hard 45% noticed
source: Simons, D. J., & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.
caveat: 2026-11-14 re-check confirmed citation and 54%/46% split; 228 people were recruited and 192 analysed after exclusions (secondary).

claim: Loftus & Palmer (1974) leading-question study.
value: Mean speed estimate (mph): smashed 40.8, collided 39.3, bumped 38.1, hit 34.0, contacted 31.8. Broken glass 'yes' one week later: smashed 16/50 (32%), hit 7/50 (14%), control 6/50
source: Loftus, E. F., & Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13(5), 585-589.
caveat: 2026-11-14 re-check: five speed means confirmed by several secondary sources (one gives 40.5 for 'smashed'); seed checked the original paper. Experiment 1 had 45 students; Experiment 2 had 150 (3 x 50).

claim: American Psychology-Law Society white paper on eyewitness identification procedures.
value: 9 recommendations (4 retained from 1998: filler selection, pre-lineup instructions, double-blind administration, confidence statement; 5 new: pre-lineup interview, evidence-based suspicion, video-recording, no repeated identification, avoid/improve showups)
source: Wells, G. L., Kovera, M. B., Douglass, A. B., Brewer, N., Meissner, C. A., & Wixted, J. T. (2020). Policy and procedure recommendations for the collection and preservation of eyewitness identification evidence. Law and Human Behavior, 44(1), 3-36.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (APA press release + Bates scholarship record). It is an AP-LS statement, not an APA policy.

claim: US National Academies report on eyewitness identification.
value: Identifying the Culprit: Assessing Eyewitness Identification (2014)
source: National Research Council (2014). Identifying the Culprit: Assessing Eyewitness Identification. National Academies Press.
caveat: Search 2026-11-14 returned no confirming result; DOI from bibliographic knowledge.

claim: Darley & Latané (1968) 'seizure' intercom study: reporting before the end of the fit.
value: 72 NYU students; alone (2-person group) 85% vs believed 4 others present (6-person group) 31%
source: Darley, J. M., & Latané, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377-383.
caveat: 85%/31% agree across sources (seed + 2026-11-14 re-check). 'Ever reported' figures differ from 'reported before end of fit'; keep the measures separate.

claim: Darley & Latané (1968) middle (3-person) condition and response latencies.
value: 62% reported before end of fit; mean latency 52 s (2-person), 93 s (3-person), 166 s (6-person)
source: Darley & Latané (1968), as reported in secondary summaries.
caveat: 2026-11-14: several secondary summaries converge on 62% (one blog misattributes it); the original PDF was listed but not readable from this session. Earlier sources quoting 64% appear to be in error.

claim: Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) forced-compliance dissonance study.
value: Enjoyment rating (-5..+5): $1 group +1.35, $20 group -0.05, control -0.45; 20 per analysed condition
source: Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203-210.
caveat: Seed-verified; 2026-11-14 re-check confirmed values in one further secondary source. Alternative explanations (self-perception, impression management) remain debated.

claim: Cowan (2001) on working-memory capacity.
value: 'A single, central capacity limit averaging about four chunks' (range 3-5), contrasted with Miller (1956) 'about seven'
source: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.
caveat: Seed row verified by orchestrator research (PubMed/primary); not re-fetched 2026-11-14.

claim: Miller (1956) 'The magical number seven, plus or minus two'.
value: Psychological Review 63(2), 81-97; separates limits on absolute judgement (bits) from immediate memory span (chunks)
source: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81-97.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (PubMed record 13310704 + MPI/SISSA records). '7 +/- 2' is a rhetorical summary; Cowan (2001) argues for ~4 chunks when rehearsal and chunking are controlled.

claim: Bridges et al. (2020) timing mega-study of 10 experiment packages.
value: Abstract: 'most of the packages achieved precision at least under 10 ms in all browsers, with PsychoPy achieving a precision under 3.5 ms in all'; audio-visual synchrony 'the least precise aspect'; results: jsPsych/Testable 3.2-8.4 ms inter-trial variability
source: Bridges, D., Pitiot, A., MacAskill, M. R., & Peirce, J. W. (2020). The timing mega-study. PeerJ, 8, e9414.
caveat: 2026-11-14 re-check confirmed the abstract quote (PeerJ, DOAJ). The 3.2-8.4 ms range is from the results section (seed). Browser RTs include a fixed lag; ZEHN must not claim lab-grade precision.

claim: International Personality Item Pool.
value: >3,000 items; >250 scales; public domain; free to copy, edit, translate
source: Goldberg, L. R., et al. (2006). The International Personality Item Pool and the future of public-domain personality measures. Journal of Research in Personality, 40, 84-96.
caveat: Seed row verified by orchestrator research (PubMed/primary); ipip.ori.org not reachable from this session on 2026-11-14 (proxy denial).

claim: IPIP 50-item Big-Five Factor Markers (Goldberg 1992 markers, IPIP version).
value: 50 items; 10 per factor; factors I Extraversion, II Agreeableness, III Conscientiousness, IV Emotional Stability, V Intellect/Imagination
source: Goldberg, L. R. (1992). The development of markers for the Big-Five factor structure. Psychological Assessment, 4(1), 26-42; IPIP item key.
caveat: Structure (10 items/factor) confirmed 2026-11-14 by secondary sources; items 1 (+E) and 2 (-A) keying confirmed via IPIP translation pages. Full verbatim list could not be fetched; see src/data/ipip.json 'verification'.

claim: PHQ-9 / GAD-7 reproduction permission.
value: 'No permission required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute'
source: Pfizer / phqscreeners.com.
caveat: Seed row verified by orchestrator research (PubMed/primary); not re-fetched 2026-11-14. ZEHN applies these screeners only to simulated clients and ships scores only.

claim: Ainsworth et al. (1978) Strange Situation classification of US (Baltimore) infants.
value: Commonly quoted ~70% secure; avoidant/resistant quoted as 15/15 OR 20/10 depending on source; Baltimore home-observation sample 26 mother-infant pairs; larger combined N (100/106) unconfirmed
source: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of Attachment. Erlbaum.
caveat: 2026-11-14: secondary sources conflict on the avoidant/resistant split (15/15 vs 20/10) and on N. Do not display a split without a 'sources conflict' badge until the 1978 book is checked.

claim: van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg (1988) cross-cultural meta-analysis of Strange Situation data.
value: 32 samples; 8 countries; N = 1,990; secure most common everywhere; intra-cultural variation ~1.5x inter-cultural variation
source: van IJzendoorn, M. H., & Kroonenberg, P. M. (1988). Cross-cultural patterns of attachment: A meta-analysis of the Strange Situation. Child Development, 59(1), 147-156.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (original article PDF listed on unife.it + Leiden repository + secondary). Pooled split (~65/21/14) appears only in secondary sources: treat as must-verify. Mostly non-US samples; few non-Western cultures.

claim: Main & Solomon added the disorganised/disoriented attachment category.
value: Described 1986; full coding procedure 1990
source: Main, M., & Solomon, J. (1990). Procedures for identifying infants as disorganized/disoriented during the Ainsworth Strange Situation. In Attachment in the Preschool Years. University of Chicago Press.
caveat: Sources give 1986 and/or 1990; chapter pages not confirmed.

claim: Baron-Cohen, Leslie & Frith (1985) Sally-Anne false-belief task.
value: 61 children (20 autistic, 14 Down syndrome, 27 typically developing); belief question passed by 85% typical, 86% Down syndrome, 20% autistic
source: Baron-Cohen, S., Leslie, A. M., & Frith, U. (1985). Does the autistic child have a 'theory of mind'? Cognition, 21(1), 37-46.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (The Transmitter + consistent secondary sources). Later work shows some autistic people pass; failure is not proof of a specific ToM deficit. ZEHN uses original characters, not the Sally-Anne dolls.

claim: Piaget's stage ages (approximate).
value: Sensorimotor ~0-2 y; preoperational ~2-7 y; concrete operational ~7-11 y; formal operational ~11 y+
source: Piaget, J. (various). Summarised in OpenStax Psychology 2e ch. 9.
caveat: 2026-11-14: only revision-note sources returned; ages are approximate and Piaget treated sequence, not age, as fundamental.

claim: McGarrigle & Donaldson 'naughty teddy' conservation study.
value: ~80 children aged ~4;10-5;10; conserved 62% (accidental teddy transformation) vs 16% (deliberate experimenter)
source: McGarrigle, J., & Donaldson, M. (1974/1975). Conservation accidents. Cognition, 3(4), 341-350.
caveat: Revision-note sources only; year given as 1974 or 1975; Moore (1986) proposed a distraction artefact.

claim: Bandura, Ross & Ross (1961) Bobo doll study design.
value: 72 children (36 boys, 36 girls) from the Stanford University nursery, aged 37-69 months; 24 per group: aggressive model, non-aggressive model, no-model control
source: Bandura, A., Ross, D., & Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575-582.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (York 'Classics' reprint of the paper + secondary). Critiques: play vs real aggression, demand characteristics, single-session lab setting.

claim: Harlow (1958) surrogate-mother studies with infant rhesus monkeys.
value: Wire vs cloth surrogates; frightened infants sought the cloth surrogate regardless of which provided milk; 'contact comfort' judged far more important than lactation
source: Harlow, H. F. (1958). The nature of love. American Psychologist, 13(12), 673-685.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (UCLA-hosted copy of the paper + EBSCO/New World Encyclopedia). Number of infants per group NOT confirmed; do not display a sample size. Serious animal-welfare criticism.

claim: Watson & Rayner (1920) 'Little Albert' fear-conditioning report.
value: Infant ~9 months at baseline tests; white rat paired with a loud noise; identity disputed (Douglas Merritte per Beck et al. 2009 vs Albert Barger per Powell et al. 2014)
source: Watson, J. B., & Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(1), 1-14.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (BPS Psychologist, Powell et al. 2014 record at MacEwan, Teaching of Psychology record). No deconditioning; generalisation claims are weak; age at conditioning (~11 months) not re-confirmed. 'failed' = never adequately replicated (single case).

claim: Henry Molaison (patient H.M.).
value: Bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 (age 27) for epilepsy; dense anterograde amnesia with preserved working and procedural memory (mirror-tracing improved over 3 days without recollection); died 2 Dec 2008, age 82
source: Scoville, W. B., & Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry, 20(1), 11-21.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (BrainFacts 2018 + PMC6007845 + AAAS). Surgery date given as 25 Aug or 1 Sep 1953. Later MRI (Corkin et al. 1997) showed a smaller lesion than Scoville estimated.

claim: Phineas Gage injury and record.
value: Injured 13 Sep 1848 near Cavendish, Vermont; tamping iron ~43 in (3 ft 7 in) long, ~1.25 in diameter, ~13.25 lb; died 21 May 1860 in San Francisco; held jobs for ~11 years after the accident
source: Macmillan, M. (2000). An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage. MIT Press; Macmillan & Kihlstrom (2019).
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Macmillan & Kihlstrom PDF, Slate 2014, Vermont sources). Published textbook accounts frequently exaggerate his behavioural change. Chile stage-coach details not confirmed this pass.

claim: Kitty Genovese murder (1964) and the '38 witnesses' story.
value: No evidence for 38 eyewitnesses who watched the whole attack and did nothing; prosecutor: about half a dozen usable witnesses; the NYT later called its reporting flawed (2016)
source: Manning, R., Levine, M., & Collins, A. (2007). The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping: The parable of the 38 witnesses. American Psychologist, 62(6), 555-562.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Lancaster EPrints record + BPS Research Digest + Poynter 2016). Exact NYT 2016 wording seen only second-hand. Bystander effect itself is a separate, lab-supported finding.

claim: Hodgkin & Huxley (1952) quantitative model of the squid giant axon; modern shifted parameters.
value: C = 1 uF/cm2; gNa = 120, gK = 36, gL = 0.3 mS/cm2; ENa = +50, EK = -77, EL = -54.4 (also -54.387) mV; rest -65 mV
source: Hodgkin, A. L., & Huxley, A. F. (1952). A quantitative description of membrane current. Journal of Physiology, 117(4), 500-544.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (PMC1392413 + Gerstner/EPFL + Nottingham lecture + NeuroWiki). Original paper used rest = 0 and reversed sign; values above are the -65 mV shifted convention. Spike threshold 6-7 uA/cm2 is a model property to be checked by A5's golden test, not a sourced fact. Nobel Prize 1963.

claim: AASM scoring manual (2007) sleep-stage nomenclature.
value: W, N1, N2, N3, R; N3 merges Rechtschaffen & Kales (1968) stages 3 and 4
source: Iber, C., et al. (2007). The AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events. AASM; Moser et al. (2009) Sleep 32(2):139-149.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (PMC2635577 + Sleep Review). EEG shown in ZEHN is labelled 'simulated EEG'.

claim: Intrinsic period of the human circadian pacemaker.
value: 24.18 h average (forced desynchrony; young and older adults), not ~25 h as earlier believed
source: Czeisler, C. A., et al. (1999). Stability, precision, and near-24-hour period of the human circadian pacemaker. Science, 284(5423), 2177-2181.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (PubMed 10381883 + Harvard Gazette + EurekAlert).

claim: 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for circadian-clock mechanisms.
value: Jeffrey C. Hall, Michael Rosbash, Michael W. Young; period (PER) gene/protein negative-feedback loop in Drosophila; timeless gene (Young, 1994)
source: Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet (2017).
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Scientific American, Bloomberg, Psychiatric News).

claim: HPA-axis stress cascade.
value: Hypothalamus CRH -> anterior pituitary ACTH -> adrenal cortex cortisol; cortisol exerts negative feedback
source: OpenStax Psychology 2e ch. 14 (Stress, Lifestyle, and Health).
caveat: Textbook-standard but the 2026-11-14 search returned no confirming source. HPA simulation in ZEHN is illustrative (labelled 'simulated').

claim: Weber's law.
value: Delta I / I = k (Weber fraction varies by modality); dated to Weber's 1834 work
source: Weber, E. H. (1834). De pulsu, resorptione, auditu et tactu; summarised in RIT 'Vision & Psychophysics' notes.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (RIT course notes + Weber-Fechner encyclopedia entry). Fails at very low/high intensities; example fractions differ between sources, so ZEHN fits k from player data.

claim: Fechner's law.
value: S = k log(I / I0); published in Elemente der Psychophysik (1860)
source: Fechner, G. T. (1860). Elemente der Psychophysik. Breitkopf & Härtel.
caveat: 2026-11-14: confirmed by encyclopedia + secondary sources (no primary access). Derived from Weber's law with extra assumptions; Stevens' power law fits magnitude estimation better.

claim: Stevens power-law exponents (psi = k * phi^a).
value: Brightness 0.33 (5 deg target, dark); loudness 0.67 (3000 Hz tone, sound pressure); visual length 1.0; electric shock 3.5 (60 Hz through fingers)
source: Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153-181; exponent table in Stevens (1975) Psychophysics.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (RIT notes table + App State exponent table + encyclopedia). Exponents depend on stimulus conditions (point-source brightness 0.5) and method; magnitude estimation itself is criticised.

claim: Hautus (1995) log-linear correction for extreme hit/false-alarm rates.
value: Add 0.5 to every cell (e.g., H = (hits + 0.5)/(signal trials + 1)); less biased than the 1/(2N) rule; always slightly underestimates population d'
source: Hautus, M. J. (1995). Corrections for extreme proportions and their biasing effects on estimated values of d'. Behavior Research Methods, Instruments, & Computers, 27(1), 46-51.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Springer PDF + sdt-metrics docs + MRC CBU wiki).

claim: Hick-Hyman law.
value: Choice RT = a + b log2(n + 1) (Hick); RT linear in transmitted information (Hyman)
source: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. QJEP, 4(1), 11-26; Hyman, R. (1953). JEP, 45(3), 188-196.
caveat: Law verified 2026-11-14 (MacKenzie/York HCI text + KSU lecture notes); page ranges and DOI from bibliographic knowledge, not re-fetched.

claim: Fitts' law.
value: MT = a + b log2(2A/W) (Fitts 1954); Shannon form log2(A/W + 1) (MacKenzie 1992)
source: Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system. JEP, 47(6), 381-391; MacKenzie, I. S. (1992). Human-Computer Interaction, 7, 91-139.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (MacKenzie York pages + Georgia Tech reading). Pages from bibliographic knowledge.

claim: WCAG 2.x Success Criterion 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A).
value: Content must not flash more than three times in any one-second period, unless below the general and red flash thresholds
source: W3C (2023). Understanding SC 2.3.1: Three Flashes or Below Threshold (WCAG 2.2).
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (W3C Understanding pages for WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2). ZEHN caps flicker at 3 Hz and offers static alternatives; the safer reading is to stay strictly below 3 flashes/s for large areas.

claim: Stroop (1935) Experiment 2 colour-naming interference.
value: Naming 100 ink colours took ~47 s longer when printed as conflicting colour words (~110 s vs ~63 s; ~74% slower)
source: Stroop, J. R. (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 18(6), 643-662.
caveat: 2026-11-14: only one secondary source gave 47 s / 74.3%; original tables not reachable. Effect itself is very robust (MacLeod 1991 review). Show figures with badge.

claim: Posner (1980) spatial cueing paradigm.
value: 'Orienting of attention' (VIIth Bartlett Lecture): valid cues speed and invalid cues slow detection
source: Posner, M. I. (1980). Orienting of attention. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 32(1), 3-25.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (two reference lists). Not to be confused with Posner, Snyder & Davidson (1980) JEP:G.

claim: Treisman & Gelade (1980) feature-integration theory.
value: Features coded pre-attentively in parallel; conjunctions need focused serial attention (search slopes)
source: Treisman, A. M., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Princeton course PDF + UT Austin copy). Strict serial/parallel dichotomy later revised (e.g., guided search).

claim: Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell (1992) attentional blink.
value: Coined 'attentional blink': impaired report of a second target shortly after the first in RSVP; deficit attentional, not sensory
source: Raymond, J. E., Shapiro, K. L., & Arnell, K. M. (1992). Temporary suppression of visual processing in an RSVP task: An attentional blink? JEP:HPP, 18(3), 849-860.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Hanover-hosted copy of paper + PMC2915904). Typical lag window (~200-500 ms) not re-confirmed; derive from player data.

claim: Cherry (1953) dichotic listening / 'cocktail party problem'.
value: Shadowing one ear's message; little content retained from the unattended ear
source: Cherry, E. C. (1953). Some experiments on the recognition of speech, with one and with two ears. JASA, 25(5), 975-979.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (two reference lists; title wording varies).

claim: Eriksen & Eriksen (1974) flanker task.
value: Incompatible flanking letters slow identification of a central target
source: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Springer special issue intro + PMC7884363).

claim: Ebbinghaus (1885) savings at retention intervals (single subject, nonsense syllables).
value: ~58% at 20 min; ~44% at 1 h; ~36% at ~9 h; ~34% at 1 day; ~28% at 2 days; ~25% at 6 days; ~21% at 31 days
source: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis. Duncker & Humblot.
caveat: 2026-11-14: only the 1-h value (44.2%) confirmed by a secondary source; other points from textbook tables. Savings is not % recalled. Show with badge.

claim: Murre & Dros (2015) replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve.
value: One subject, ~70 h of learning; intervals 20 min, 1 h, 9 h, 1 day, 2 days, 31 days; curve replicated, with a possible upward jump at 24 h
source: Murre, J. M. J., & Dros, J. (2015). Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve. PLOS ONE, 10(7), e0120644.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (DOAJ + UvA DARE + FORRT replication atlas).

claim: Glanzer & Cunitz (1966) two storage mechanisms in free recall.
value: Filled (counting) delays of 0, 10 or 30 s: primacy preserved, recency reduced/abolished at 30 s
source: Glanzer, M., & Cunitz, A. R. (1966). Two storage mechanisms in free recall. JVLVB, 5(4), 351-360.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (citation in multiple sources; delay values consistent across secondary summaries). Use 'reduced or eliminated' wording.

claim: Brown-Peterson distractor paradigm.
value: Trigram recall after counting backwards for 3-18 s (Peterson & Peterson 1959); independently Brown (1958)
source: Peterson, L. R., & Peterson, M. J. (1959). Short-term retention of individual verbal items. JEP, 58(3), 193-198; Brown, J. (1958). QJEP, 10(1), 12-21.
caveat: Peterson & Peterson citation verified 2026-11-14; Brown (1958) not found in search (citation from knowledge). Decay interpretation later challenged by proactive-interference findings (Keppel & Underwood 1962).

claim: Peterson & Peterson (1959) recall by delay.
source: Peterson & Peterson (1959), via secondary summaries.
caveat: Secondary study guides agree; original figure not seen. Show with badge.

claim: Craik & Lockhart (1972) levels-of-processing framework.
value: Retention is a function of depth of encoding (structural < phonemic < semantic)
source: Craik, F. I. M., & Lockhart, R. S. (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. JVLVB, 11(6), 671-684.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Springer/PBR reference lists). Criticised for circular definition of 'depth'.

claim: Roediger & McDermott (1995) DRM false-memory paradigm.
value: Lists of associates of an unpresented critical lure produce high false recall and recognition of the lure
source: Roediger, H. L., III, & McDermott, K. B. (1995). Creating false memories. JEP:LMC, 21(4), 803-814.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (UNL VAMP lab PDFs + Frontiers 2020).

claim: Roediger & McDermott (1995) critical-lure recall rate.
value: ~40% (Exp. 1) / ~55% (Exp. 2) false recall of critical lures
source: Roediger & McDermott (1995).
caveat: Not confirmed by 2026-11-14 search; values from textbook knowledge. Show with badge.

claim: Rescorla-Wagner (1972) model of Pavlovian conditioning.
value: Delta V_X = alpha_X * beta * (lambda - sum V); predicts blocking and asymptotic acquisition
source: Rescorla, R. A., & Wagner, A. R. (1972). A theory of Pavlovian conditioning. In A. H. Black & W. F. Prokasy (Eds.), Classical Conditioning II (pp. 64-99). Appleton-Century-Crofts.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (BibSonomy + OrDB + CRAN calmr vignette + hosted PDF). Fails to predict e.g. latent inhibition and spontaneous recovery.

claim: Yerkes & Dodson (1908) original experiment.
value: Dancing mice; white/black box discrimination with shock of varying strength; optimal shock depended on discrimination difficulty. The general arousal-performance 'inverted U' is a later generalisation (Teigen 1994)
source: Yerkes, R. M., & Dodson, J. D. (1908). The relation of strength of stimulus to rapidity of habit-formation. J Comp Neurol Psychol, 18(5), 459-482; Teigen, K. H. (1994). Theory & Psychology, 4(4), 525-547.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (York 'Classics' text + Teigen 1994 record + secondary). ZEHN's Yerkes-Dodson curve is labelled 'illustrative'.

claim: Shepard & Metzler (1971) mental rotation of 3-D objects.
value: Same/different RT increased linearly with angular disparity (0-180 deg), picture-plane and depth rotations alike
source: Shepard, R. N., & Metzler, J. (1971). Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects. Science, 171(3972), 701-703.
caveat: Linearity verified 2026-11-14 (multiple sources).

claim: Shepard & Metzler (1971) rotation rate.
value: ~60 deg/s (~1 s per 60 deg); intercept ~1 s
source: Shepard & Metzler (1971), as commonly cited.
caveat: Not confirmed 2026-11-14. ZEHN reports the player's own slope rather than a reference value.

claim: Wason selection task.
value: Wason (1966, 1968); typically fewer than ~10% choose the logically correct card pair in the abstract version
source: Wason, P. C. (1968). Reasoning about a rule. QJEP, 20(3), 273-281.
caveat: Task attribution confirmed 2026-11-14 (Wason obituary, Johnson-Laird); the <10% rate and journal pages not confirmed. ZEHN uses original card content.

claim: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) framing ('Asian disease') problem.
value: Gain frame (N = 152): 72% chose the sure option A; loss frame (N = 155): 78% chose risky option D
source: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1981). The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice. Science, 211(4481), 453-458.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (NCSU-hosted and Gwern-hosted copies of the paper). ZEHN uses original wording, not the 'Asian disease' text.

claim: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) anchoring with a 'wheel of fortune'.
value: Anchor 10 -> median estimate 25%; anchor 65 -> median 45% (African UN member countries)
source: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Chapman 2002 chapter + Cambridge 'Heuristics and Biases').

claim: Facial Action Coding System.
value: Ekman & Friesen (1978) FACS, Consulting Psychologists Press; revised 2002 with Hager
source: Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1978). Facial Action Coding System: Investigator's Guide; Ekman, Friesen & Hager (2002).
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (reference lists + guide copyright notice). FACS manual is copyrighted: ZEHN uses AU numbers/names only, with original procedural faces.

claim: Flynn effect meta-analysis (Trahan et al. 2014).
value: 285 studies since 1951 (N = 14,031): mean gain 2.31 IQ points per decade; 2.93 for modern Stanford-Binet/Wechsler norms
source: Trahan, L. H., Stuebing, K. K., Fletcher, J. M., & Hiscock, M. (2014). The Flynn effect: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 140(5), 1332-1360.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (PMC4152423). Some countries now show a reversed ('negative') Flynn effect.

claim: Flynn (1987) gains across 14 nations.
value: IQ gains of 5-25 points in a single generation across 14 nations
source: Flynn, J. R. (1987). Massive IQ gains in 14 nations. Psychological Bulletin, 101(2), 171-191.
caveat: One secondary source only (2026-11-14).

claim: Ranehill et al. (2015) robustness test of power posing.
value: N = 200 (102 men, 98 women) vs original N = 42; no effect on testosterone, cortisol or risk-taking; self-reported feeling of power did increase
source: Ranehill, E., et al. (2015). Assessing the robustness of power posing. Psychological Science, 26(5), 653-656.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (Univ. Zurich hosted paper + UZH news + Healio). Original: Carney, Cuddy & Yap (2010) Psychol Sci 21(10). Ronay et al. (2017) also null.

claim: Wagenmakers et al. (2016) RRR of the pen-in-mouth facial-feedback study.
value: 17 labs; pooled rating difference 0.03 units, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.16] vs original 0.82 on a 10-point scale
source: Wagenmakers, E.-J., et al. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917-928.
caveat: Upgraded 2026-11-14 (APS page + UvA + Lancaster records). Total N (~1,894) not confirmed. Strack argued video-recording may have altered the effect.

claim: Coles et al. (2022) Many Smiles Collaboration.
value: N = 3,878 from 19 countries; facial mimicry and voluntary smiling increased happiness; pen-in-mouth evidence inconclusive
source: Coles, N. A., et al. (2022). A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration. Nature Human Behaviour, 6, 1731-1742.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (HAL + ScienceDaily + several university repositories). Effect sizes not captured here.

claim: Sherif's Robbers Cave study (1954).
value: Two groups of ~11-year-old boys at an Oklahoma summer camp; competition then superordinate goals; group size usually quoted as 22
source: Sherif, M., Harvey, O. J., White, B. J., Hood, W. R., & Sherif, C. W. (1961). Intergroup Conflict and Cooperation: The Robbers Cave Experiment.
caveat: 2026-11-14: setting confirmed; N = 22 not confirmed. See F-PERRY for critique.

claim: Perry (2018) archival critique of Robbers Cave.
value: An earlier 1953 camp at Middle Grove did not support the hypothesis and was not reported; staff interventions; researchers acted as a third group
source: Perry, G. (2018). The Lost Boys: Inside Muzafer Sherif's Robbers Cave Experiment. Scribe.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (Australian Book Review + BPS Psychologist + Dublin Review of Books). Perry's interpretation is itself debated.

claim: Systematic review of mental-health literacy research in Pakistan.
value: 613 records screened; 59 studies included; measures heterogeneous with limited validity; no meta-analysis possible
source: Munawar, K., Abdul Khaiyom, J. H., Bokharey, I. Z., Park, M. S.-A., & Choudhry, F. R. (2020). A systematic review of mental health literacy in Pakistan. Asia-Pacific Psychiatry, 12(4), e12408.
caveat: Verified 2026-11-14 (NTU and IIUM repositories + PubMed 32803860).

claim: Review of barriers/facilitators to mental-health service access in Pakistan.
value: 13 studies; barriers: cost, stigma, low knowledge, prior side-effects/dissatisfaction, distance/time, reliance on traditional/religious healers, low social support; facilitators: trust in services, recognising seriousness
source: Review in International Journal of Mental Health (2021). Authors not confirmed.
caveat: Abstract content seen via search snippet 2026-11-14; author list and title not confirmed.

claim: Faith-healer consultation among psychiatric patients in Karachi.
value: ~32% of patients at one Karachi hospital had ever visited a faith healer
source: [instructor to add verified source]
caveat: Seen only as a secondary mention; single-hospital sample, citation unknown. Must NOT be shown until an instructor adds a verified source.

claim: Umang Pakistan mental-health helpline.
source: Umang contact page; WHO EMRO MHPSS suicide page.
caveat: Hours may vary — verify before calling. Number appears on Umang's own contact page and WHO EMRO (search 2026-11-14). Hours conflict: 24/7 (Umang social media, Tribune), daily 3-11 pm (worldhotlines.org), weekdays 9-5 (anxiety.pk). Umang states it does not handle active suicide attempts: call 115/1122 or go to the nearest emergency department.

claim: Taskeen mental-health helpline.
source: Taskeen (taskeen.org) via directories.
caveat: Hours may vary — verify before calling. Number appears in several directories but was not seen on taskeen.org itself (2026-11-14). Hours conflict: Mon-Sat 11 am-11 pm (seed, from Taskeen site), Mon-Fri 9 am-12 am (dawaai.pk), weekdays 9-5. Taskeen states it does not diagnose.

claim: Rozan Counselling Helpline.
value: 0304-111-1741 (also helpline@rozan.org)
source: Rozan (rozan.org/rozan-counselling-helpline).
caveat: Hours may vary — verify before calling. Number on Rozan's own pages. Hours conflict even within rozan.org: one page headline '10AM to 8PM | Seven Days a Week', another 'weekdays 09:00-17:00 (Ramadan 10-6)'; TherapyRoute: Mon-Fri 09:30-17:00. Normal call charges apply.

claim: Pakistan emergency numbers.
value: Police 15; Rescue/ambulance 1122 (provincial; coverage varies); Edhi ambulance 115; Fire 16
source: UN Women Asia-Pacific; Government of Canada travel advice; Punjab government pages.
caveat: Hours may vary — verify before calling. 2026-11-14: 15/1122/115 consistent across sources; 112 from mobile may not work reliably; Rescue 1122 coverage differs by province.

claim: Federal health helpline 1166 (Sehat Tahaffuz) with 'Humraaz' mental-health service.
value: 1166; Humraaz app + helpline launched April 2023
source: Dawn (Apr 2023); Express Tribune (Apr 2023); UNICEF Pakistan.
caveat: Hours may vary — verify before calling. Launch confirmed by Dawn and Tribune; current availability of the mental-health option is unclear (UNICEF 2026 describes 1166 mainly as immunisation/general health). Referral line, not counselling. Callers should ask whether Humraaz is available.

claim: International fallback directory.
value: Find A Helpline (findahelpline.com), linked by IASP; Befrienders Worldwide (befrienders.org)
source: Find A Helpline; IASP.
caveat: Hours may vary — verify before calling. Not re-fetched 2026-11-14 (host unreachable from session). Opening it requires network access; ZEHN shows the URL as text only.

claim: Anthropic model IDs for the optional LLM mentor.
value: claude-sonnet-5-5 (default), claude-opus-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5
source: Anthropic API model list.
caveat: claude-opus-5-5 matches the model ID of the agent session that wrote this file; sonnet/haiku IDs NOT confirmed (docs not reachable). A7 must keep the model field user-editable.
